items.correctExplanation: True — weighted mixes let totals contradict every subgroup. The paradox is arithmetic, not error.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. Subgroup losses plus lopsided weights manufacture overall wins routinely.
items.lessonContent:
Totals can contradict all their parts through weighting.
Never trust a total without its subgroup table.
Weighting is the hidden author of rankings.
Share this: demand subgroup tables behind one ranking.
items.question: A treatment can trail in every subgroup yet lead overall.
items.title: The Total Contradiction

items.correctExplanation: False — overall rates weight subgroups by size. Simple averages ignore the weights and mislead.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. Totals blend subgroups by patient counts; unweighted averages answer a different question.
items.lessonContent:
Averages come weighted or worthless in grouped data.
Ask for the weights behind every blended rate.
Simple means of rates mislead systematically.
Share this: weight one average correctly today.
items.question: Overall success rates are simple averages of their subgroup rates.
items.title: The Simple Average

items.correctExplanation: False — the 87.5% crowns patient mix, not healing. Subgroup tables show B trailing twice.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. B's overall lead rides mild-case volume; per-severity tables favor A both times.
items.lessonContent:
Headline rates crown mixes as often as merit.
Per-severity tables judge healers fairly.
Populations served shape scores earned.
Share this: split one medical headline by severity.
items.question: An 87.5% overall cure rate against 80% proves the higher-rated treatment heals individuals better.
items.title: The Healing Crown

items.correctExplanation: True — with identical subgroup sizes, totals must agree with subgroup direction. Symmetry of weights removes the trick.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. Equal denominators turn totals into honest averages that follow their parts.
items.lessonContent:
Equal mixes keep totals truthful.
Balance denominators before trusting blends.
Fair comparisons need matched weights.
Share this: check one comparison's subgroup sizes.
items.question: With equal subgroup sizes, overall comparisons always agree with subgroup comparisons.
items.title: The Balanced Scales

items.correctExplanation: False — department patterns explained the gap; no unit discriminated. Application mix manufactured disparity.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. Women applied to tougher departments; within departments rates matched.
items.lessonContent:
Disparity in totals never alone proves discrimination.
Selection patterns mimic bias with precision.
Audit applications before verdicts.
Share this: explain selection effects to one friend.
items.question: The Berkeley totals proved gender bias in admissions.
items.title: The Berkeley Verdict

items.correctExplanation: True — severe-case hospitals absorb the hardest patients and sink in totals while excelling per ward.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. Case severity, not skill, orders such leaderboards; risk adjustment reverses them.
items.lessonContent:
Toughest caseloads sink the finest hospitals.
Rank healers within severity bands only.
Courage in intake looks like failure in totals.
Share this: defend one severe-case hospital's stats.
items.question: A hospital can rank last overall while delivering the best care in every ward.
items.title: The Punished Healer

items.correctExplanation: False — reversals need only lopsided weights, achievable in dozens of cases. Small tables flip too.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. A 290-to-30 split fits in hundreds of patients; magnitude of imbalance matters, not sample size.
items.lessonContent:
Imbalance, not bigness, births reversals.
Small studies flip as readily as censuses.
Watch ratios between groups, not headcounts.
Share this: flip one toy example with lopsided groups.
items.question: Simpson reversals require thousands of cases to appear.
items.title: The Thousand Myth

items.correctExplanation: False — schedules inflate averages; the higher number may own the softer slate. Split by difficulty first.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. Weak-pitching volume can crown the weaker bat; averages inherit opponents.
items.lessonContent:
Averages inherit schedules silently.
Strength-of-schedule adjusts every honest ranking.
Soft slates mint hollow crowns.
Share this: adjust one average for its schedule.
items.question: The higher batting average always identifies the better hitter.
items.title: The Hollow Crown

items.correctExplanation: True — subgroup tables expose the weighting trick. Disaggregate first, conclude second.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. Splitting by severity, department, or venue dissolves the illusion into arithmetic.
items.lessonContent:
Disaggregation is the universal solvent of reversals.
Split before you conclude, always.
Tables with subgroups tell truth; totals tell tales.
Share this: split one puzzling ranking this week.
items.question: Comparing within subgroups resolves Simpson reversals.
items.title: The Split Cure

items.correctExplanation: False — it is exact arithmetic of weighted averages. Mystery dissolves into denominators.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. No law of numbers breaks; weights simply outvote rates.
items.lessonContent:
Paradoxes of aggregation obey arithmetic perfectly.
'Paradox' here means surprise, never impossibility.
Trust the math while distrusting the headline.
Share this: demo one reversal with pocket change.
items.question: Simpson reversals violate the laws of arithmetic.
items.title: The Broken Math

items.correctExplanation: True — enrollment skews rewrite efficacy headlines. Populations tested shape percentages published.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. Mild-heavy trials flatter weak drugs; severity tables restore order.
items.lessonContent:
Trial populations co-author every efficacy claim.
Read enrollment tables beside result tables.
Medicine's fine print lives in demographics.
Share this: read one trial's enrollment mix.
items.question: Trial populations alone can reverse which drug looks better.
items.title: The Enrolled Illusion

items.correctExplanation: False — that universal claim is exactly what the paradox refutes. Weights can overturn unanimous subgroups.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. Unanimous subgroup wins still bow to lopsided weights; totals answer a different question.
items.lessonContent:
'Every part' never guarantees 'the whole' in weighted worlds.
Emergence of totals defies part-wise logic.
 wholes obey weights; parts obey rates.
Share this: quote one unanimous-parts reversal.
items.question: Beating a rival in every subgroup guarantees beating them overall.
items.title: The False Guarantee

items.correctExplanation: True — rates set the ceiling; weights choose the seat. Reversals are weighting events.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. Identical rates with different mixes still reverse; mixes alone suffice.
items.lessonContent:
Weights write outcomes rates merely propose.
Find the weighting before debating the rates.
Denominators decide more than numerators.
Share this: name the weights behind one rate.
items.question: Unequal group weights, not differing rates, drive Simpson reversals.
items.title: The Weight Engine

items.correctExplanation: True — matched denominators let honest winners emerge. Controls earn trust through balance.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. Balanced wards and classes remove weighting tricks, leaving merit visible.
items.lessonContent:
Balanced designs are paradox-proof by construction.
Match denominators when testing rivals fairly.
Controls confirm what reversals deny.
Share this: praise one balanced comparison today.
items.question: Equal-mix control comparisons confirm honest rankings.
items.title: The Fair Control

items.correctExplanation: False — an 8-point total gap can ride pure application mix. Margins measure mixes too.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. Berkeley-style weighting manufactures such gaps without any unit-level edge.
items.lessonContent:
Margins in totals measure mixes plus merit inseparably.
Eight points of mix look exactly like eight of skill.
Decompose gaps before awarding laurels.
Share this: decompose one gap into mix and merit.
items.question: A 63%-to-55% overall gap proves one group's superiority.
items.title: The Eight-Point Proof

items.correctExplanation: False — swapping labels swaps winners but never the mechanism. Math ignores names.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. The reversal follows weights; A and B are passengers, not drivers.
items.lessonContent:
Mechanisms outlive their labels in every paradox.
Rename parties and watch math stand still.
Loyalty belongs to logic, never labels.
Share this: retell one paradox with swapped names.
items.question: Swapping the group labels changes the underlying mathematics.
items.title: The Swapped Names

items.correctExplanation: True — populations average; patients particularize. Your denominator is your destiny.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. Overall crowns serve crowds; subgroup wins serve the person matching them.
items.lessonContent:
Personal choices demand personal denominators.
Crowd averages misadvise individuals routinely.
Match your subgroup, then choose.
Share this: choose one service by subgroup today.
items.question: Individual decisions should follow the decision-maker's subgroup, not the overall rate.
items.title: The Personal Denominator

items.correctExplanation: True — bull-year clustering manufactures legends from luck. Calendars compound into reputations.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. Inception dates and bull runs write records managers merely sign.
items.lessonContent:
Calendars co-manage every fund's record.
Split returns by market weather first.
Luck compounds exactly like skill — briefly.
Share this: check one star fund's birth date.
items.question: Bull-market clustering alone can fake a star manager's record.
items.title: The Calendar Legend

items.correctExplanation: False — territories and lead quality shape boards as much as talent. Quotas ignore terrain.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. Warm-lead volume crowns Mediocrity over mastery; normalize before crowning.
items.lessonContent:
Leaderboards blend terrain with talent invisibly.
Territory is the silent commission partner.
Adjust terrain before judging closers.
Share this: ask what turf fed one top seller.
items.question: Sales leaderboards always measure selling talent.
items.title: The Terrain Board

items.correctExplanation: False — bigger samples preserve lopsided weights perfectly. Volume never balances ratios.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. Millions of rows with 10-to-1 mixes reverse as crisply as hundreds.
items.lessonContent:
Volume preserves proportions; it never repairs them.
Big data with skewed mixes misleads at scale.
Balance beats bigness in grouped comparisons.
Share this: distrust one massive unbalanced ranking.
items.question: Collecting more data eliminates Simpson reversals.
items.title: The Big Data

items.correctExplanation: True — short-hop networks flatter every carrier's total. Maps confound punctuality systematically.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. Route length, not crew skill, often orders on-time tables.
items.lessonContent:
Networks write rankings crews merely inherit.
Compare route to route, never carrier to carrier.
Maps are the fine print of punctuality.
Share this: split one delay ranking by route.
items.question: Airline route maps systematically confound punctuality rankings.
items.title: The Route Map

items.correctExplanation: False — department application patterns can manufacture firm-wide gaps. Pools precede prejudice in the audit order.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. Self-selection into tough departments mimics discrimination in totals precisely.
items.lessonContent:
Audit pools before alleging prejudice.
Selection effects forge perfect counterfeits of bias.
Order matters: applications first, decisions second.
Share this: demand pool data behind one gap claim.
items.question: Firm-wide hiring gaps prove discrimination by themselves.
items.title: The Pool Defense

items.correctExplanation: True — enrollments, not teaching alone, order league tables. Intake confounds instruction.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. Junior-heavy schools ride easy cohorts to unearned laurels.
items.lessonContent:
Intake shapes outcomes schools merely channel.
Compare cohorts, never crests, in education.
Enrollment is destiny's first draft.
Share this: unmask one league table's intake.
items.question: School league tables partly reflect student intake rather than teaching alone.
items.title: The Intake Effect

items.correctExplanation: True — hierarchical Simpson nests reversals within reversals. Splitting twice can flip twice.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. Sub-subgroups can overturn subgroup verdicts exactly as subgroups overturn totals.
items.lessonContent:
Aggregation deceives at every level of nesting.
Split recursively until verdicts stabilize.
Depth of analysis must match depth of grouping.
Share this: split one table twice and watch it flip.
items.question: A reversal can itself reverse inside finer sub-subgroups.
items.title: The Nested Flip

items.correctExplanation: False — honest weighting manufactures reversals without fraud. Arithmetic needs no villain.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. Lopsided case loads flip totals innocently; blame the mix, not the makers.
items.lessonContent:
Innocent mixes convict honest counters daily.
Reserve fraud claims for tampered counts.
Most paradoxes are accidents of aggregation.

items.question: Discovering a Simpson reversal means somebody cooked the numbers.
items.title: The Innocent Flip
